articles.headline: Six Popular Sweeteners Linked to Brain Aging Equivalent to 1.6 Years
articles.body: A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62 percent faster decline in memory and thinking skills. The researchers tracked adults in Brazil over eight years, examining seven common sweeteners including aspartame, saccharin, and erythritol. Six of the seven were linked to faster cognitive decline, particularly memory loss. Adults under 60 and those with diabetes showed the strongest effects. The study was observational and couldn't prove causation, but the magnitude of decline mirrors aging an extra 1.6 years.
articles.takeaway: If you're reaching for diet sodas or sugar-free products daily, consider cutting back. The cognitive impact may not be worth the calorie savings.

articles.headline: Thirty Minutes in a Sauna Floods Your Bloodstream With Immune Cells
articles.body: A Finnish study found that a single 30-minute sauna session, including a brief cold shower midway through, temporarily increases circulating white blood cells including lymphocytes and neutrophils. The immune cells surge into circulation from tissues where they normally reside, positioning them to patrol the body more effectively. Blood samples showed the increase was most pronounced immediately after the session, then normalized within 30 minutes. The response mirrors the immune activation seen during exercise. This isn't about creating new immune cells but mobilizing existing ones to higher alert status.
articles.takeaway: A regular sauna habit may give your immune surveillance a temporary boost. It's not a replacement for exercise, but it offers a passive way to activate your defenses weekly.

articles.headline: Daily Peanuts Boost How Your Aging Brain Responds to Insulin
articles.body: Researchers at Maastricht University found that eating 60 grams of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts daily for 16 weeks improved insulin responsiveness in memory-related regions of the brain's right hemisphere. Thirty-one healthy adults aged 60 to 75 participated in a crossover study comparing peanut consumption against a control period of avoidance. The improvement showed up on brain imaging in clusters including the hippocampus. Peanuts contain L-arginine, unsaturated fats, and fiber that may support the effect. The study measured insulin sensitivity changes, not direct memory performance or dementia prevention.
articles.takeaway: Two servings of peanuts daily may help sustain brain function as you age. Pair them with other brain-healthy habits for a real edge.

articles.headline: Less Than 42 Minutes of Bright Daylight Daily Tied to Higher Dementia Risk
articles.body: A large study of 87,577 adults wearing light sensors found that those exposed to more than 1,000 lux of daylight during the day had 16 percent lower dementia risk than those in dimmer conditions. Over 8.1 years of follow-up, 741 participants developed dementia. Participants with even brighter exposure of 5,000 lux or more saw additional risk reduction. Researchers accounted for sleep, exercise, obesity, and other known risk factors. Machine learning ranked bright daytime light as a stronger dementia predictor than alcohol use, hearing loss, or trauma. Vitamin D did not explain the relationship, suggesting other pathways are at play.
articles.takeaway: Make morning and midday daylight exposure a non-negotiable habit. Forty-two minutes is the floor. Get outside early, and take daylight breaks during your workday.

workout.title: Threshold Tempo Ladder: Progressive Race-Pace Sustainability
workout.tip: Use perceived exertion to dial in pace rather than obsessing over GPS. During tempo blocks, you should be able to speak only short phrases (4–5 words max). If you can sing, you're too easy; if you can't speak at all, you're too hard.
workout.warmup: 10 min easy Z2 jog, 5×20 sec buildout strides (accelerate each stride) with 90 sec recovery jog between each

exercises.name: Easy Aerobic Primer
exercises.notes: Z2 conversational pace, HR 60–70% max. Establish smooth cadence (170–180 rpm), relax shoulders, feel your rhythm.

exercises.name: Tempo Ladder Block 1
exercises.notes: Tempo/threshold pace (Z4, HR 85–88% max). This is your half-marathon goal pace or just below marathon goal pace. Stay controlled and smooth.

exercises.name: Recovery Jog
exercises.notes: Easy Z2. HR drops 10–15 bpm. Mental reset. Optional light fueling: 25–50 cal carbs if needed.

exercises.name: Tempo Ladder Block 2
exercises.notes: Maintain Z4 tempo pace (85–88% HR max). The ladder lengthens effort duration—your mind must settle into the discomfort. Focus on relaxed arms and steady breathing.

exercises.name: Recovery Jog
exercises.notes: Easy Z2. Let HR recover fully. Consume 50 cal carbs if available. Prepare mentally for the final, longest block.

exercises.name: Tempo Ladder Block 3 (Peak Effort)
exercises.notes: Sustain Z4 tempo pace (85–88% HR max). This is the mental crescendo—the longest tempo block. Legs will feel heavy; this is the adaptation stimulus. Breathe deeply, hold form.

exercises.name: Cool-Down Easy Jog
exercises.notes: Z2 easy pace. Gradually bring HR down. Celebrate pushing through sustained effort.

workout.cooldown: 5 min walking, then: standing quad stretch 40 sec each leg, hamstring fold 60 sec, glute figure-4 45 sec each side, calf stretch 30 sec each leg. Refuel with 20–30g protein + 40–60g carbs within 30 min of completion.
workout.description: A 75-minute structured long run using a ladder format to build lactate threshold and race-pace endurance without excessive fatigue. Athletes warm into three progressive tempo efforts (7, 9, and 11 minutes) at half-marathon or marathon goal pace with brief recovery jogs between, developing mental toughness and pacing consistency under fatigue. Perfect for intermediate marathon and Olympic-distance triathlon athletes building aerobic power and race-specific speed.

meal.title: Teriyaki Salmon Onigiri (Japanese Rice Balls)
meal.description: Flaked teriyaki-glazed salmon folded into warm sushi rice and shaped into portable rice balls—an authentic, carb-rich pre-workout fuel with 30g protein that travels well and sits light in your stomach before a brick session or long run.
meal.instructions:
1. Pan-sear salmon over medium heat for 5–6 minutes per side until cooked through; flake into small pieces.
2. In a small bowl, mix soy sauce and mirin; toss flaked salmon in the glaze.
3. Divide warm sushi rice into two portions (makes 2 rice balls).
4. Press one portion of rice into a wet hand, create a small indent, fill with 1 tbsp teriyaki salmon, top with another layer of rice, and gently shape into a ball.
5. Repeat with second portion.
6. Sprinkle with sesame seeds and a pinch of salt.
meal.tip: Make these the night before and store in plastic wrap at room temperature or cool—they stay fresh for 24 hours and are easy to grab before a long training block. The rice provides fast carbs while the salmon protein prevents stomach upset.
